newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma to Washington for "uneasy" talks.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma to Washington for "uneasy" talks.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, struggling to defend his former Soviet republic against charges of stalled reforms and widespread corruption, flies to Washington on Wednesday for talks with U.S. officials.
Kuchma will inaugurate a Ukrainian-American Commission on cooperation, jointly chaired with U.S. Vice-President Al Gore.
"My trip will be within the framework of the Kuchma-Gore Commission. This will be the first such meeting," Kuchma told reporters this week. "This is not going to be an easy trip."
Kuchma is also due to meet the leaders of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and will ask both institutions for money to close the budget gap and back economic reforms.
But Kiev analysts said Kuchma would not have an easy task.

"The U.S. and the West in general are worried about economic indicators. Gross Domestic Product is falling, low inflation is rather artificial and more than 12 million people have not been paid for months," said Olexander Razumkov, head of the Independent Centre for Political and Economic Research.
"The West has pumped significant credits into Ukraine and is worried about whether Ukraine will be able to repay them."
Western criticism of Ukraine centres on allegations of widespread corruption, an unstable investment climate and mountains of red tape.

"We are increasingly concerned that the Ukrainian government has been unable to implement the ambitious reform agenda developed in cooperation with the IMF late last year," the Group of Seven industrialised countries said last month.
"We urge the government to engage fully and quickly to implement this package while this window of opportunity remains open," the strongly worded statement added.
Kuchma's chief of staff Yevhen Kushnaryov said Kuchma would try to give as clear a picture as possible.
"The aim is to give real information to the U.S. leadership and financial institutions about reforms and what is going on with this bad thing...I mean corruption," he said.
"It (corruption) exists, no one is hiding it, but the propaganda around this and the will to portray some American companies as victims of brutality is overestimated," he added.
Some U.S. legislators have threatened to reduce or cancel aid to Ukraine unless it eliminates corruption.
Kiev is the third world's largest recipient of U.S. aid after Egypt and Israel and is due to receive $330 million in U.S. grants and $650 million in loans this year.

Kuchma is also due to discuss security issues, including a future treaty with the Western NATO alliance, but is set to resist likely U.S. demands that Ukraine stop production of middle- and short-range missiles. Washington fears these can be sold to states like Libya, Iraq and Iran.
"Our position is firm," Kuchma said. "We are not going to build a strategic partnership only on one-side compromises."
Kuchma's visit to Washington precedes a possible visit to Kiev from Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
Yeltsin is expected to visit Ukraine on May 30. The visit, already postponed half a dozen times, could point to warmer relations between the neighbour states.
